R4.2.response:
Thank you for setting out precisely what would make the evaluation convincing. We have done all four things, and the live proof of concept produced the clearest evidence in the paper.

On the proof of concept with live traffic: the detector now runs inside a controller process speaking OpenFlow 1.3 to an Open vSwitch datapath under Mininet, with three hosts on 100 Mbit links, an attacker running a randomised-source SYN flood from hping3, a benign client running iperf3 and ping against a server, and the whole thing measured in three conditions. With no detector the flood costs the benign client 73 percent of its throughput, which falls from 95.39 to 25.78 Mbit/s. With the detector it costs nothing measurable: 95.29 to 95.39 Mbit/s, zero added packet loss, and no rise in round-trip time. The switch holds 997 drop rules against distinct spoofed sources by the end of the attack, against four flow entries and no drop rules undefended. The undefended condition uses the same controller with detection disabled, so the comparison isolates the detector rather than the presence of a controller.

On controller CPU and memory: 101 percent of one core and 190 MB resident with detection enabled, against 32.5 percent and 58 MB for the learning switch alone. On end-to-end detection latency: 10.84 ms at the median, rising to 13.12 ms when every admitted alert is also attributed. On QoS impact: none measurable in the emulated network, and separately, on the socket testbed where the controller is driven past saturation, benign background flows see their 95th-percentile round-trip time rise by a factor of 1.21.

The run also produced a result we had not anticipated: mitigation pays for its own control-plane cost. Packet-in events reaching the controller fall from 40,160 undefended to 2,335 with detection enabled, because the installed rules stop the flood at the switch and the controller stops seeing it.

On the explainability cost you quote, the submitted figures were optimistic. Attributing every alert reduces sustained throughput to 661 flows/s, not 1,953. We define the explanation trigger formally and measure three budget policies against it; attributing one representative per attack episode restores 35,652 flows/s with every alert still carrying an attribution by reference. Section VII-K reports the frontier and states the interpretive cost of the policy that recovers the most throughput.

On the deep-learning comparison: a 1D-CNN, an LSTM, a Transformer encoder, a reconstruction autoencoder and a graph neural network are all run under the same protocol, on the same splits, on the CPU, with the same harness. The strongest reaches macro F1 0.9102 against 0.9706 for the detector. The autoencoder is the most instructive row and we report it in full: trained on benign traffic as the method requires, it assigns lower reconstruction error to attack flows than to benign ones, giving ROC-AUC 0.0073. That is not an implementation defect. A randomised SYN flood is more repetitive than benign traffic, so a model fitted to benign flows reconstructs the attack better than its own training distribution. The premise of reconstruction-based anomaly detection is false on a corpus where the attack is 97 percent of the traffic.

A short video of the emulated session is submitted as supplementary material, showing the topology coming up, the flood starting, the drop rules being installed, and the benign client's traffic continuing throughout. Every frame is output from the running system.

We should also say what this does not establish. It is a three-host emulation. It cannot exhibit multi-datapath rule distribution, controller failover, or the traffic patterns of an operational fabric, and the limitations section says so rather than leaving the scale to be inferred.
R4.2.action: Added a Mininet and Open vSwitch testbed with live traffic in three conditions, reporting controller CPU, memory, end-to-end detection latency, flow-table occupancy and QoS impact; added the explanation-budget study that replaces the submitted throughput figures; added five deep-learning baselines under one protocol; and submitted a video of the session as supplementary material.
